title: 03. Databases & Data Modeling: MySQL
summary: MySQL is the world's most widely-deployed open-source relational database, powered by the InnoDB storage engine (MVCC + clustered index + crash-safe redo log), with binary log (binlog) for replication and PITR, GTID for…
objectives: How does InnoDB's clustered index differ from PostgreSQL's heap+index design?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** MySQL is the world's most widely-deployed **open-source relational database**, powered by the **InnoDB storage engine** (MVCC + clustered index + crash-safe redo log), with **binary log (binlog)** for replication and PITR, **GTID** for deterministic replication topology, **semi-synchronous replication** for low-data-loss HA, and **InnoDB Cluster** (Group Replication + MySQL Router + MySQL Shell) for managed multi-primary or single-primary HA — favored by **Facebook, Uber, and Instagram** for web-scale OLTP where simple point-lookup throughput and operational familiarity outweigh PostgreSQL's feature edge.

MySQL's history shapes its strengths. Built in 1995 by Swedish company MySQL AB (later acquired by Sun, then Oracle), MySQL prioritized speed and simplicity over ANSI-SQL compliance and advanced features — early versions didn't even have transactions (the MyISAM engine was non-transactional). When InnoDB (a transactional engine) became the default in MySQL 5.5 (2010), MySQL gained ACID transactions, MVCC, and crash safety, while keeping its speed advantage on simple queries. This legacy — fast for the 95 % case, feature-light for the 5 % — made MySQL the default for web applications in the 2000s: Wikipedia, Facebook, WordPress, Reddit, and most of the LAMP stack ran on MySQL. Even today, after PostgreSQL has largely caught up on performance, MySQL's footprint in production is enormous — Facebook alone runs tens of thousands of MySQL instances, and many "new" databases (TiDB, PlanetScale's Vitess, AWS Aurora MySQL) are MySQL-wire-compatible to leverage this installed base.

The **InnoDB storage engine** is the heart of modern MySQL. Unlike PostgreSQL's single storage layer, MySQL has a pluggable storage engine architecture: InnoDB (default, transactional), MyISAM (legacy, non-transactional), Memory (in-memory hash tables), NDB (Cluster — distributed), and others (RocksDB via MyRocks). In practice, everyone uses InnoDB except for special cases (Facebook used MyRocks for compression). InnoDB's design: (1) **Clustered index** — the table's primary key IS the data; rows are stored in a B+Tree ordered by PK. Secondary indexes store the PK value (not a row pointer), so looking up via a secondary index requires two lookups (find PK, then find row by PK). (2) **MVCC via undo logs** — when a row is updated, InnoDB writes the new version in place and writes the old version to an undo log. Concurrent readers reconstruct the old version from the undo log. (This differs from PostgreSQL's approach of keeping multiple versions in the table itself — InnoDB's approach uses less space but undo log growth can slow reads.) (3) **Redo log (ib_logfile)** — like PostgreSQL's WAL, ensures crash-safe durability. Writes are appended to the redo log (sequential I/O), and data pages are flushed later. (4) **Doublewrite buffer** — writes pages to a contiguous area before scattering them to their final locations, protecting against partial-page writes (a half-written 16 KB page during a crash would otherwise corrupt the database).

The **binary log (binlog)** is MySQL's equivalent of PostgreSQL's WAL — but with important differences. The binlog records logical changes (statement-based or row-based) at the server level, while the redo log records physical page changes at the engine level. The binlog is used for: (1) **Replication** — a replica connects to the primary, downloads binlog events, and applies them. (2) **Point-in-time recovery** — restore from a backup, then replay binlog up to a chosen timestamp. (3) **CDC (Change Data Capture)** — tools like Debezium parse the binlog to stream changes to Kafka, Elasticsearch, or a data warehouse. Binlog formats: **STATEMENT** (logs the SQL statement — small, but non-deterministic functions like `NOW()` or `RAND()` cause replica divergence), **ROW** (logs the actual row changes — large, but deterministic; the modern default), **MIXED** (statement for safe queries, row for non-deterministic). Real-world: Debezium + MySQL binlog is the standard CDC pipeline at most companies; Netflix uses it to stream changes from MySQL OLTP to Snowflake for analytics.

**GTID (Global Transaction Identifier)** solves a chronic MySQL replication pain: tracking position. Without GTID, replication is tracked by binlog file + position (e.g., "replica is at mysql-bin.000123:4567"), which is fragile — if the primary fails over, the new primary has a different binlog sequence, and replicas must be manually re-pointed with the right position. GTID assigns each transaction a unique ID (`server_uuid:sequence_number`) that's stable across the topology. A replica can be re-pointed to any primary by saying "I've applied up to GTID X; please send me everything after." This makes failover, replication topology changes, and upgrades much simpler — tools like Orchestrator and MaaS use GTID for automatic failover. GTID has been default-recommended since MySQL 5.6 (2013); any modern MySQL deployment should have it enabled.

**Semi-synchronous replication** is MySQL's middle ground between async and sync replication. In pure async (the default), the primary commits and returns to the client immediately; the replica catches up later — fast, but data loss on failover. In **semi-sync**, the primary waits for at least one replica to ack receipt of the binlog event (not application, just receipt) before returning COMMIT to the client. This guarantees the binlog event is on at least two hosts — zero data loss for committed transactions, with minimal latency penalty (one network round-trip). MySQL offers two semi-sync modes: **AFTER_SYNC** (default in 5.7+, the primary acks after the replica receives but before applying — the classic "lossless" semi-sync) and **AFTER_COMMIT** (the older mode, less safe). Real-world: Facebook, Slack, and many large MySQL deployments use semi-sync with 2-3 replicas; if all replicas are down, semi-sync degrades to async (configurable timeout) to avoid blocking the primary.

**InnoDB Cluster** is MySQL's answer to managed HA. It bundles three components: (1) **Group Replication** — a multi-primary or single-primary replication group using Paxos-like consensus for writes; members automatically coordinate, detect failures, and elect new primaries. (2) **MySQL Router** — a thin proxy that routes client traffic to the right cluster member (primary for writes, any member for reads); clients connect to the router, not directly to MySQL. (3) **MySQL Shell** — an admin tool for cluster setup, monitoring, and failover. InnoDB Cluster provides: automatic failover (typically 10-30 seconds), read/write splitting, and consistency levels (`GROUP_REPLICATION_CONSISTITY = BEFORE_ON_PRIMARY_FAILOVER` etc.). Trade-offs: Group Replication caps write throughput at what the consensus group can agree on (slower than async); requires low latency between members (same region); max 9 members. For higher scale, **Vitess** (now a CNCF project, used by YouTube, Slack, Square) shards MySQL horizontally and presents a single logical database — PlanetScale is a managed Vitess service.

Real-world: **Facebook/Instagram run the world's largest MySQL fleet** — tens of thousands of instances, petabytes of data. Their architecture (documented in Uber Engineering's blog and Facebook's MySQL patches): (1) **Schema-tier sharding by user_id** — Facebook's social graph is split across thousands of MySQL shards by `user_id % N`; no cross-shard joins. (2) **`UNION ALL` of shard queries** — fetching a user's news feed fans out to N shards in parallel and merges results. (3) **Custom MySQL patches** — Facebook and Uber both maintain MySQL forks with patches for their specific workloads (Uber: faster semi-sync, schema changes; Facebook: compression via MyRocks, atomic DDL). (4) **Semi-sync + Geo-replication** — each shard has a primary in one DC, semi-sync replicas in the same DC, and async cross-region replicas for DR. Uber famously migrated from PostgreSQL back to MySQL in 2016 (Uber Engineering blog post "Why Uber Engineering Switched from Postgres to MySQL") — their reasons included PostgreSQL's MVCC bloat issues for update-heavy workloads, Postgres's replication limitations (pre-10 logical replication was painful), and the engineering team's familiarity with MySQL. The post was controversial — PostgreSQL advocates argued the issues were operational, not fundamental — but it's a real-world data point on MySQL at scale.

Real-world: **WhatsApp runs on MySQL** (with FreeBSD) — Erlang for the app tier, MySQL for durable storage of user metadata, messages, and groups. WhatsApp's deployment handles billions of users with a small engineering team, leveraging MySQL's operational simplicity and FreeBSD's network performance. The takeaway: MySQL is battle-tested at unprecedented scale if you shard horizontally and tune carefully.

(MVCC snapshots)"] InnoDB -->|"doublewrite buffer"| DW["Doublewrite
(crash safety)"] MySQL -->|"binlog (logical)"| Binlog["Binary log
ROW/STATEMENT/MIXED"] Binlog -->|"stream to replica"| Replica1["Replica 1
(semi-sync, acks)"] Binlog -.->|"stream async"| Replica2["Replica 2
(async, lag ~50ms)"] Binlog -->|"CDC"| Debezium["Debezium"] Debezium --> Kafka["Kafka"] Kafka --> Snowflake["Snowflake (analytics)"] GTID["GTID
server_uuid:seq"] -.->|"stable across topology"| Replica1 GTID -.-> Replica2 ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` InnoDB clustered index (table = PK B+Tree): Secondary index Clustered index (= data) +----------------+ +----------------+ | email | PK | | PK | row data | +-------+--------+ +----+-----------+ | a@x | 42 | ----> | 42 | alice,... | | b@x | 17 | | 17 | bob,... | | c@x | 99 | | 99 | carol,... | +-------+--------+ +----+-----------+ (2 lookups: email->PK, then PK->row) vs PostgreSQL (heap + separate indexes): Secondary index Heap (data) +----------------+ +---------------+ | email | rowptr | ----> | rowptr | row | +-------+--------+ +--------+------+ InnoDB: 1 lookup if PK, 2 if secondary PostgreSQL: 1 lookup (any index points to heap) Replication topology (GTID + semi-sync): Primary (DC1) Replica1 (DC1, semi-sync) Replica2 (DC2, async) +----------+ +-----------+ +-----------+ | binlog: | --semi-sync-> | binlog: | | binlog: | | GTID 1 | ack "got 1" | GTID 1 | --async-repl-> | GTID 1 | | GTID 2 | --semi-sync-> | GTID 2 | (lag ~50ms) | GTID 2 | | GTID 3 | ack "got 3" | GTID 3 | | (catching)| +----------+ +-----------+ +-----------+ | v (ack from R1 received -> return COMMIT to client) | Client Semi-sync guarantees: committed txn is on >=2 hosts (zero data loss) Latency cost: +1 RTT per commit (typically <1ms same-DC) ``` ### Walkthrough 1. A client transaction modifies rows: InnoDB writes the change to the redo log (fsync for durability), updates the in-memory buffer pool, and writes the old version to the undo log (so concurrent readers can reconstruct it — MVCC). On COMMIT, the binlog records the logical change (row-based by default), and the redo log + binlog are fsynced together (two-phase commit between engine and binlog). 2. The binlog is streamed to replicas. With semi-sync, the primary waits for at least one replica to ack receipt before returning COMMIT to the client (zero data loss, ~1 RTT latency). With async, the primary returns immediately and replicas catch up later (small data-loss window on failover). GTIDs track position so replicas can be re-pointed across failovers. 3. CDC tools (Debezium) parse the binlog and stream row-level changes to Kafka for downstream consumers (Elasticsearch, Snowflake, cache invalidation). This decouples analytical workloads and search indexing from the OLTP database — MySQL stays fast for OLTP, the warehouse handles analytics.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- MySQL feature mock using sqlite3 (which mimics InnoDB-style SQL).
- sqlite3 PRIMARY KEY creates a B-tree index, but rows live in the B-tree leaves (clustered).
- CREATE TABLE users ( user_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, -- clustered: data in B-tree email TEXT UNIQUE, -- secondary: stores PK name TEXT, balance INTEGER )
- Mock MySQL binlog: ordered list of (GTID, event) entries.
- 1. InnoDB-style clustered index demo
- Primary-key lookup: 1 B-tree descent
- Secondary-index lookup: 2 B-tree descents
- (find PK by email, then find row by PK)

**Defines:** `demo_clustered_index()`, `Binlog`, `MySQLPrimary`, `Replica`, `CDCConsumer`

```python
"""
MySQL feature mock using sqlite3 (which mimics InnoDB-style SQL).
Demonstrates: clustered PK, secondary index 2-lookup, binlog/GTID
concepts, semi-sync replication acks, and a CDC-style binlog tail.

Run:  python3 mysql_demo.py
"""

import sqlite3
import json
import time
import threading
from collections import deque

# ---------- 1. InnoDB-style clustered index demo ----------
def demo_clustered_index():
    """sqlite3 PRIMARY KEY creates a B-tree index, but rows live in the
    B-tree leaves (clustered). Demonstrate the 2-lookup cost on a
    secondary index by separating the 'table' (heap) from the index."""
    print("=== 1. Clustered index vs secondary index (InnoDB-style) ===")
    conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
    conn.execute("""
        CREATE TABLE users (
            user_id  INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,   -- clustered: data in B-tree
            email    TEXT UNIQUE,           -- secondary: stores PK
            name     TEXT,
            balance  INTEGER
        )
    """)
    conn.executemany("INSERT INTO users VALUES (?,?,?,?)", [
        (42, "alice@x.com", "Alice", 1000),
        (17, "bob@x.com", "Bob", 500),
        (99, "carol@x.com", "Carol", 200),
    ])
    conn.commit()

    # Primary-key lookup: 1 B-tree descent
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(1000):
        r = conn.execute("SELECT name,balance FROM users WHERE user_id=?",
                         (42,)).fetchone()
    pk_ms = (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000

    # Secondary-index lookup: 2 B-tree descents
    # (find PK by email, then find row by PK)
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(1000):
        r = conn.execute("SELECT name,balance FROM users WHERE email=?",
                         ("alice@x.com",)).fetchone()
    sk_ms = (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000

    print(f"  PK lookup (1 B-tree descent):    {pk_ms:.2f} ms / 1000 ops")
    print(f"  Secondary idx (2 B-tree descents): {sk_ms:.2f} ms / 1000 ops")
    print("  -> PK lookups are slightly faster (1 vs 2 B-tree descents)")

# ---------- 2. Binlog + GTID ----------
class Binlog:
    """Mock MySQL binlog: ordered list of (GTID, event) entries."""

    def __init__(self, server_uuid):
        self.server_uuid = server_uuid
        self._seq = 0
        self.events = []        # list of (gtid, event_dict)
        self._subscribers = []  # replica/cdc callbacks

    def append(self, event):
        self._seq += 1
        gtid = f"{self.server_uuid}:{self._seq}"
        entry = (gtid, event)
        self.events.append(entry)
        # Notify subscribers (replicas, CDC)
        for cb in self._subscribers:
            cb(entry)
        return gtid

    def subscribe(self, callback):
        self._subscribers.append(callback)

class MySQLPrimary:
    """Mock primary: executes SQL, writes binlog with GTIDs."""

    def __init__(self, server_uuid):
        self.binlog = Binlog(server_uuid)
        self.data = {}   # table -> {pk: row}

    def insert(self, table, pk, row):
        self.data.setdefault(table, {})[pk] = row
        gtid = self.binlog.append({
            "op": "INSERT", "table": table, "pk": pk, "row": row,
        })
        return gtid

    def update(self, table, pk, new_row):
        old = self.data[table][pk]
        self.data[table][pk] = new_row
        gtid = self.binlog.append({
            "op": "UPDATE", "table": table, "pk": pk,
            "before": old, "after": new_row,
        })
        return gtid

    def delete(self, table, pk):
        old = self.data[table].pop(pk)
        gtid = self.binlog.append({
            "op": "DELETE", "table": table, "pk": pk, "before": old,
        })
        return gtid

# ---------- 3. Semi-sync replication ----------
class Replica:
    """Mock replica: subscribes to binlog, acks receipt (semi-sync)."""

    def __init__(self, name, mode="semi-sync"):
        self.name = name
        self.mode = mode
        self.applied_gtid = None
        self.acked_gtid = None
        self.data = {}
        self.acks = []   # list of GTIDs acked (for semi-sync)

    def callback(self, entry):
        gtid, event = entry
        # Semi-sync: ack immediately on receipt (before apply)
        if self.mode == "semi-sync":
            self.acked_gtid = gtid
            self.acks.append(gtid)
        # Apply (simulate apply latency)
        time.sleep(0.001)
        if event["op"] == "INSERT":
            self.data.setdefault(event["table"], {})[event["pk"]] = event["row"]
        elif event["op"] == "UPDATE":
            self.data[event["table"]][event["pk"]] = event["after"]
        elif event["op"] == "DELETE":
            self.data[event["table"]].pop(event["pk"], None)
        self.applied_gtid = gtid

# ---------- 4. CDC consumer (Debezium-style) ----------
class CDCConsumer:
    """Mock Debezium: tails binlog, publishes to Kafka topic."""

    def __init__(self, topic):
        self.topic = topic
        self.messages = deque()

    def callback(self, entry):
        gtid, event = entry
        self.messages.append({
            "topic": self.topic,
            "key": f"{event['table']}:{event['pk']}",
            "value": event,
            "gtid": gtid,
        })

# ---------- Demo ----------
if __name__ == "__main__":
    demo_clustered_index()

    print("\n=== 2. MySQL primary + binlog + GTID ===")
    primary = MySQLPrimary("3E2F1A-aaaa-bbbb-cccc-dddddddddddd")

    # Subscribe a semi-sync replica
    replica1 = Replica("replica-1", mode="semi-sync")
    primary.binlog.subscribe(replica1.callback)

    # Subscribe an async replica (simulated)
    replica2 = Replica("replica-2", mode="async")
    primary.binlog.subscribe(replica2.callback)

    # Subscribe a CDC consumer
    cdc = CDCConsumer("mysql.users")
    primary.binlog.subscribe(cdc.callback)

    g1 = primary.insert("users", 42, {"email": "alice@x.com", "balance": 1000})
    print(f"  INSERT -> GTID {g1}")
    print(f"    replica-1 acked: {replica1.acked_gtid} (semi-sync)")
    print(f"    replica-2 acked: {replica2.acked_gtid}")
    print(f"    replica-1 applied: {replica1.applied_gtid}")
    print(f"    replica-1 data: {replica1.data}")

    g2 = primary.update("users", 42, {"email": "alice@x.com", "balance": 900})
    print(f"  UPDATE -> GTID {g2}")
    print(f"    replica-1 data after apply: {replica1.data}")

    g3 = primary.delete("users", 42)
    print(f"  DELETE -> GTID {g3}")
    print(f"    replica-1 data after apply: {replica1.data}")

    print("\n=== 3. CDC pipeline (Debezium-style) ===")
    print(f"  Kafka topic '{cdc.topic}' received {len(cdc.messages)} messages:")
    while cdc.messages:
        m = cdc.messages.popleft()
        print(f"    [{m['gtid']}] {m['value']['op']:6s} {m['key']}: {m['value']}")
    print("  -> CDC decouples OLTP from analytics/search")
    print("     (Snowflake/Elasticsearch consume from Kafka, not MySQL)")
```

quiz.question: How does InnoDB's clustered index differ from PostgreSQL's heap+index design?
options: With AFTER_SYNC (lossless) semi-sync, the primary waits for the replica to ack receipt of the binlog event BEFORE committing locally.
MySQL's binlog is the gold standard for CDC — every row change is in the binlog (ROW format), parseable in real time.
MySQL InnoDB doesn't release disk space back to the OS when rows are deleted — it marks the space as free for reuse, but the file stays the same size.
In InnoDB, the table's primary key IS the data — rows are stored in the leaves of a B+Tree ordered by PK.
quiz.explanation: In InnoDB, the table's primary key IS the data — rows are stored in the leaves of a B+Tree ordered by PK. This is called a "clustered index." Secondary indexes (on email, created_at, etc.) don't point to the row directly; they store the PK value, so a secondary-index lookup requires two B+Tree descents: (1) find the PK by the secondary key, (2) find the row by PK in the clustered index.
